units.unit: Claim will be about whether tighter rent control makes life better or worse for SDU residents
A source would need to show what happened to rents, living conditions, or number of units when rules were introduced
Will argue about number of units and rents
Guess: tighter control could push landlords to take units off the market, hurting tenants
A source on that would be evidence for my view
D6 models supply and welfare effects of rent control, matching my guess about landlords removing units
D7 is a real case of a rent freeze to see if it happened
D2 has actual numbers on stock and rents in Hong Kong
Guess about landlords removing units looks right for hard caps
D6p1 says a 10 percent cut removes 3 to 5 percent of stock
Berlin D7p1 shows supply shrinking
D2p1 shows Hong Kong stock kept growing under the 2021 ordinance
D6p2 says the 2021 ordinance only limits increases
Tightening should not mean hard caps
If tenants care more about not being evicted than the rent number, my focus on rent levels is too narrow
Tightening increase limits within a tenancy is a kind of tenure security, fitting what tenants want better than a hard cap
The landlord source would push against my claim that tighter increase limits are safe for supply
To matter, it would need to show landlords actually exiting or raising rents or evicting in response to the 2021 ordinance, not just complaining
D5 is the landlord view, needed to test whether tighter limits make owners exit
D11 gives the tenant view on tenure security versus caps
Skipping D10 because it is marked not for circulation
D5 threatens exit but D5p3 admits no margin data and a self-reported survey with 34 percent response, so I trust it less
D2p1 (stock still growing) backs that exit has not happened so far
D11p1 says 61 percent of tenants would trade rent for three-year security, supporting my answer to the opposing view
Position: tighten with tenure security and a light band on initial rents, but no hard cap
Hong Kong should tighten narrowly: tenure security and a light limit on initial rents, no hard cap
Hard caps shrink supply by 3 to 5 percent per 10 percent rent cut (D6p1)
Berlin showed the cost lands on outsiders (D7p3)
The 2021 increase-limit rule did not stop stock growing (D2p1)
A light band on initial rents fits tenants only if it is small
D11p3 itself supports tenure security plus a light band, so the survey says rent ranks below security and queue length, not that it is irrelevant
Less sure how strong the survey is since D11 only surveyed 440 households
Will use claim, evidence, objection, reply structure
Claim is narrow tightening; evidence is D6, D7 and D2
Objections are the landlord exit threat (D5) and that rents are not the real problem (D11)
Reply is that tenure security plus a light band answers both
D2p3 says post-2023 data is extrapolated, so I will say stock growth is only solid to 2023
D2p2 shows SDU rents rose 3.1 percent under the ordinance versus 1.7 percent for general rents
Rent burden went from 31 to 34 percent
Current control has not fully protected tenants, so tighten rather than leave it alone
D2p2 sits under the case for tightening at all
D5 argues against a hard initial-rent cap, not against increase limits
D5 admits it has no margin data (D5p3)
Exit is a real risk for a hard cap, which I already reject, but not shown for a light band
Keep the band light because owners also face compliance costs (D5p1)
A source for the light band should show small limits do not push owners out
D2p1 helps because stock grew under the increase limits
That is a different rule than an initial-rent band, so I will say so honestly
D11p2 says enforcement capacity spent on rents is not spent on inspecting fire and ventilation
That is a cost of tightening I should admit
A light band still needs enforcement, so it should be simple
D6p3 says households that lose units are the same people a cap tries to protect
Use D6p3 to explain why I reject hard caps
Use D11p1 to explain why security matters more to tenants than the rent number
Weakest points are D11's 440 households and D2's post-2023 extrapolation
I will state both weak points
D8 is a second-generation scheme with light first-rent regulation
D8 is the closest real example of my narrow tightening idea
New York is a light scheme and stock contraction is modest (D8p2)
Tenants stay longer in New York, which is tenure security
D8p3 warns the 2019 tightening was linked to fewer listings and weaker maintenance
Even a light tightening has costs, and I should say that
Place the enforcement point as a limit on the light band
The band should be simple and rely on written tenancy agreements
The weakest tenants are missed first
Handle D11's small sample first: 440 households is modest but matches the NGO's own recommendation
I will call D11 supporting, not decisive
If enforcement is weak, protection lands last on those with no written agreement
Tenure security should require a written tenancy
Cannot cite the inspection minute since I have not read it, so state it as my own reasoning
I am answering D5, not conceding it fully
D5's exit threat is real for a hard cap, but D5p3 admits it has no margin data
D8p3 is a limit I place on the band: keep it light because New York's tightening was linked to fewer listings
